paragraphs: This paper describes a working neural computing system built around radial basis functions and a mixture of analog and digital hardware. Its central design choice is to divide the network across two kinds of circuitry: custom analog circuits handle the input layer, while a digital signal processing board handles the hidden and output layers.

The division is intended to combine low power consumption with control over overall system error. Rather than treating the hardware implementation as a single uniform technology choice, the system assigns different network stages to different components. The contribution therefore includes both a neural network implementation and a concrete way to organize its computation across hardware types.

The authors report fabricating and testing the analog circuits, assembling the complete system, and running several applications. For one remote sensing problem, the system produced substantially better results than previously obtained with conventional methods. That application supports the usefulness of the completed design, alongside its stated power and error advantages.
neurips-1993-a-hybrid-radial-basis-funct.tldr: A working radial basis function neurocomputer combines analog and digital hardware for low power use and improved remote sensing results.

paragraphs: This paper demonstrates supervised learning in an analog chip whose recurrent neural network evolves continuously over time. The network contains six neurons and 42 adjustable connection strengths and thresholds. Its task is to produce changing outputs that approximate supplied periodic signals, so learning concerns the network's temporal behavior as well as its output values.

The chip learns by applying random perturbations to its parameters and observing how the error changes along those directions. Those observations guide adjustments that reduce error. The hardware integrates the learning functions and generation of pseudorandom perturbations, and it also supports teacher forcing and long-term storage of parameters that would otherwise be volatile.

In the reported experiment, the network learned a circular trajectory at 1 kHz in 100 seconds. The chip occupies a 2 mm by 2 mm area, uses a 2 μm CMOS process, and dissipates 1.2 mW. Together, these results demonstrate that a small analog recurrent circuit can learn to generate a specified periodic dynamical pattern.
neurips-1993-a-learning-analog-neural-ne.tldr: A small analog recurrent neural chip learns periodic output dynamics through integrated random-perturbation training.

paragraphs: This paper asks how to describe continuous-time neural systems when their components do not operate on a single synchronized schedule. The motivation spans mathematical modeling, analog hardware, and distributed simulation. In each setting, understanding asynchronous behavior requires a precise account of when individual components evolve and when information passes between them.

The authors introduce such a definition for dynamical systems expressed through ordinary differential equations. Their formulation uses local times and communication times, separating a component's own progress from the timing of exchanges with other components. This gives a mathematical basis for studying asynchrony within systems ordinarily described using continuous time.

The paper then provides preliminary convergence results for contractive and monotone systems. These results address conditions under which asynchronous dynamics still approach their limiting behavior from across the system's state space. Applying the analysis to neural networks yields conditions under which additive-type networks can be made asynchronous. The contribution is therefore a framework and conditional convergence guarantees, rather than a claim that every continuous-time network tolerates arbitrary asynchrony.
neurips-1993-asynchronous-dynamics-of-co.tldr: A mathematical framework identifies conditions under which continuous-time neural networks retain convergence when operating asynchronously.

paragraphs: This paper distinguishes two possible targets for Bayesian neural network training: the most probable weight vector and the most probable input-output function. A weight vector specifies the network's adjustable numbers, whereas an input-output function describes the behavior those numbers produce. The paper argues that the conventional Bayesian interpretation of backpropagation addresses the first target.

To optimize the probability of the function instead, the author derives an additional correction term for backpropagation. This matters because changing the object whose probability is maximized changes the learning objective. The result connects a question about what Bayesian learning should select to a concrete modification of the training procedure.

The correction favors functions that admit shorter descriptions. In particular, it encourages some forms of feature selection, pruning, and weight sharing, linking these structural choices to the function-level Bayesian objective. The qualification matters: the abstract does not claim that every version of those techniques follows from the correction. Its central finding is that a preference for compact functional descriptions emerges when inference targets network behavior.
neurips-1993-bayesian-backpropagation-ov.tldr: Optimizing Bayesian probability over network functions requires a backpropagation correction that favors compact descriptions and certain structural simplifications.

paragraphs: This paper examines research questions raised by specialized hardware for connectionist modeling, meaning computation with neural network models. The arrival of dedicated connectionist supercomputers makes the relationship between network methods and computing architecture an issue in its own right. The abstract presents several disputed design questions rather than a single algorithm or experimental result.

One question concerns how efficiently these machines can implement incremental learning. Supporting a network's computations and supporting its learning procedure are related requirements, and the paper identifies the latter as a point of controversy. Another question is whether networks need dynamic reconfiguration, making changes to network organization part of the discussion about hardware capabilities.

The paper also highlights programming environments: specialized machines need ways for researchers to express and work with their models. Taken together, these topics connect learning methods, network organization, and software support. The contribution described in the abstract is an agenda for evaluating parallel neural computing platforms through the modeling activities they must support.
neurips-1993-connectionist-modeling-and-.tldr: The paper identifies contested learning, reconfiguration, and programming requirements for specialized parallel neural computing hardware.

paragraphs: This paper studies the classification capacity of multilayer perceptrons whose first hidden layer contains threshold logic units. It considers dichotomies, or assignments of input points to two classes, and gives a counting result for point configurations that occur with positive probability under random selection. The aim is to connect network structure with the number of classifications it can represent.

The analysis also yields a connectivity requirement when the number of points exceeds the product of input dimension and first-layer width. In that setting, the stated result requires every first-layer unit to connect to all inputs. The resulting maximal capacities, in Cover's sense, are twice the input dimension per hidden unit and two input patterns per synaptic weight.

The abstract states that single-hidden-layer networks attain both capacities, which match the corresponding single-neuron values. Comparing these results with estimates of VC dimension reveals a difference between capacity notions: for sufficiently large input dimension and hidden-layer width, VC dimension exceeds Cover's capacity. Thus, the theoretical measure chosen affects how network classification capacity is characterized.
neurips-1993-counting-function-theorem-f.tldr: A counting theorem relates multilayer classification capacity to connectivity and shows that VC dimension can exceed Cover's capacity.

paragraphs: This paper models self-organization in recurrent networks by allowing both neuron states and their interactions to change. The neurons take binary values, while their symmetric connections have continuous values and evolve in response to neuronal activity. The central assumption is a separation of timescales: neuronal changes happen much faster than connection changes.

Because of that separation, the neurons can be treated as effectively at Boltzmann equilibrium on the timescale of the slower interactions. The authors derive an effective statistical-mechanical description whose partition function involves an average over replicated versions of the system. This resembles the replica method used for spin glasses, but the replication parameter has a different status.

Here, the number of replicas represents a ratio of two temperatures and can vary over real values. It therefore has a physical interpretation within the model rather than serving only as a mathematical device. The abstract reports phase consequences as this ratio and external stimuli change, and states that the framework can extend to other models.
neurips-1993-coupled-dynamics-of-fast-ne.tldr: Separating fast neuronal activity from slow connection changes yields a statistical-mechanical model with a physically meaningful replica parameter.

paragraphs: This paper uses minimum description length to learn representations that are economical to describe while preserving enough information to reconstruct the input accurately. Its distinctive idea is that a highly redundant population of active neurons can still have a compact description. What matters is the structure of the collective activity, rather than simply how many units participate.

Each hidden unit receives a position in a low-dimensional implicit space. Training encourages their activities to form a bump with a standard shape in that space. Once the shape is fixed, its center provides a cheap way to describe the activity pattern. An autoencoder's input-to-hidden weights are adjusted to create these structured responses.

The hidden units' positions are learned too, giving the representation flexibility beyond adjusting connection weights. With different input classes, the network develops a discontinuous topography. Because the population code occupies a learned space distinct from the original input space, it can express nonlinear, higher-order input properties while retaining a compact description of its activity.
neurips-1993-developing-population-codes.tldr: Minimum description length trains redundant population codes whose activity can be compactly described by a bump's location in a learned space.

paragraphs: The researchers used optical recordings to map orientation preference and ocular dominance in five infant macaques aged 3.5 to 14 weeks. These maps describe cortical preferences for visual orientation and input from either eye. Basic features of both maps, together with relationships between them, were already robust at the youngest age examined.

Development nevertheless changed some aspects of the maps. Ocular dominance signals strengthened, and the spacing between ocular dominance bands increased steadily across the age range. The authors interpret the spacing change as evidence that neonatal cortical growth contributes to the eventual adult spacing of these bands.

Orientation preference spacing did not show a corresponding increase. This difference raises the possibility that some cells change orientation preference as the cortical surface expands. The early presence of relationships between the two map types also favors the possibility of an innate developmental process without extensive visual experience. These are interpretations supported by the observed patterns, rather than direct demonstrations of cell preference changes or experience-independent development.
neurips-1993-development-of-orientation-.tldr: Infant macaques already show organized visual cortical maps, while subsequent growth affects ocular dominance spacing differently from orientation spacing.

paragraphs: This paper develops a computational account of the Mauthner system, a brainstem circuit that triggers rapid escape responses to sounds in teleost fish. Its focus is the circuit's function in directional hearing. The modeling task connects a sensory signal to a fast behavioral response through a network constrained by the biological system.

The authors use backpropagation to train a feedforward neural network with realistic constraints. Those constraints are important to the purpose of the simulations: the resulting network behavior should be interpretable in terms of the circuit being studied. Learning provides a way to generate candidate explanations for how activity within that circuit supports its function.

The simulations produce hypotheses that can be expressed directly in terms of auditory nerve fibers, the system's principal cells, and associated inhibitory neurons. This is the central reported outcome. The network serves as a source of biologically interpretable hypotheses, connecting a computational description of directional hearing to activity in identifiable parts of the escape circuit.
neurips-1993-directional-hearing-by-the-.tldr: A biologically constrained neural simulation generates interpretable hypotheses about the fish brainstem circuit responsible for sound-triggered escapes.

paragraphs: This paper introduces a fast method for reducing the dimension of data while capturing nonlinear structure. It builds a locally linear description by combining principal component analysis with clustering. The key organizational choice is to describe different portions of the data with local models, allowing the overall representation to go beyond a single linear description.

A new distortion measure connects the clustering process with the construction of those local models. Distortion expresses how much the encoding loses or alters the data under the method's criterion. Bringing clustering and linear modeling together makes the grouping of examples part of the representation-learning procedure, rather than treating the two operations as unrelated tasks.

Experiments on speech and image data compare the method with five-layer auto-associative networks. The local linear approach produces encodings with lower distortion and trains more than an order of magnitude faster. The reported advantage therefore concerns both representation quality and training effort in those experiments, supporting local linear modeling as a practical approach to nonlinear dimension reduction.
neurips-1993-fast-non-linear-dimension-r.tldr: Combining clustering with local PCA yields lower-distortion encodings and substantially faster training than the tested five-layer auto-associative networks.

paragraphs: This paper addresses classification when supervisory labels are unavailable or costly, as can happen in autonomous robotics or models of human learning. Labels normally make it possible to measure and reduce training misclassifications directly. The proposed substitute uses relationships between the distributions of patterns received through different sensory modalities.

Separate networks process the modalities, and training seeks to reduce disagreement between their outputs. The authors show that this agreement objective is a sensible approximation to minimizing each network's classification errors and produces similar results. The useful learning signal therefore comes from how the different sources of sensory information relate to one another.

On the Peterson-Barney vowel dataset, the method finds suitable positions for codebook vectors, the representatives used to organize the patterns. It works particularly well when the classes that are difficult to distinguish differ between modalities. That finding explains why complementary sensory information matters: ambiguity in one modality need not coincide with ambiguity in the other, making agreement informative for learning a classification.
neurips-1993-learning-classification-wit.tldr: Networks can learn classifications without labels by reducing disagreement across sensory modalities, especially when their ambiguities differ.

paragraphs: This paper addresses dynamical systems that operate in multiple modes of behavior. Such systems create a modeling and control problem because their behavior is not described by one unchanging mode. The authors extend the mixture-of-experts architecture so that a collection of controllers can work within a model of these changing operating conditions.

The extension is based on a Markov process model, which represents transitions between modes. It leads to a recurrent gating network that manages a set of linear or nonlinear controllers. Recurrence makes the gating mechanism part of the system's temporal processing, connecting the choice of controller with a description of how modes change over time.

The authors demonstrate that the architecture can learn effective control strategies for both jump-linear and nonlinear plants with multiple behavioral modes. Here, a plant is the system being controlled. The stated result supports combining specialized controllers with a temporal model of mode changes, bringing the organization of the controller set into the learning problem.
neurips-1993-mixtures-of-controllers-for.tldr: A Markov-based recurrent gating network learns to coordinate controllers for dynamical systems with multiple operating modes.

paragraphs: This paper revisits what a protein secondary-structure predictor should predict. The usual task assigns local amino acid sequences to alpha helix, beta strand, or coil, but the authors describe the accuracy of neural predictions for these conventional classes as disappointing. They investigate whether different structure classes can be more predictable from local sequence.

The method uses two neural networks that evolve together while examining sequence and structure data. Rather than holding the target categories fixed throughout learning, it develops new secondary-structure classes alongside the ability to predict them. This makes the definition of the classification problem part of the learning process itself.

The resulting classes are substantially more predictable from local amino acid sequence than the conventional categories. They retain some similarities to helix, strand, and coil while also differing from them. The improvement therefore concerns a learned structural classification, and its meaning depends on that changed target. The contribution is a way to discover structure categories that align more closely with information available in local sequence.
neurips-1993-neural-network-definitions-.tldr: Two co-evolving networks discover protein structure categories that local amino acid sequences predict more accurately than conventional categories.

paragraphs: This paper considers learning an input-output relationship by actively exploring it. Learning the kinematics or dynamics of a robotic manipulator provides the motivating example. In this setting, the learner influences which observations become available through the actions it chooses, so the exploration strategy is part of the learning problem.

The argument rests on an explicit resource assumption: actions are expensive while computation is cheap. Under that assumption, it makes sense to spend computation selecting an informative trajectory through the input space. The objective is to obtain as much information as possible while taking as few exploratory steps as possible.

The author discusses how optimal experiment design can guide this choice and demonstrates the approach on a simple kinematics problem. The significance is the connection between planning an experiment and planning exploration: both involve choosing observations for the information they provide. The demonstration applies that principle to learning a mapping, with the value of the approach tied to the stated imbalance between action and computation costs.
neurips-1993-neural-network-exploration-.tldr: Optimal experiment design guides informative exploration when collecting observations through actions is more expensive than computation.

paragraphs: This paper examines whether the behavior seen in a computer simulation reflects the true dynamics of a neural network. The issue is framed in terms of corrupted pseudo-orbits: simulated sequences that contain perturbations rather than following the system's mathematical evolution exactly. The authors use observability to describe the connection between these sequences and genuine network behavior.

For discrete-time analog neural networks, they prove global observability except possibly on small exceptional sets. In the sense stated by the abstract, corrupted simulation trajectories still reflect the network's true dynamical behavior. The exception is part of the theorem's scope and distinguishes the result from an unconditional guarantee for every analog network case.

For locally finite discrete Boolean networks, the paper gives an observability result without exceptions. The two findings provide mathematical support for interpreting simulated neural dynamics despite corruption in the simulated trajectories. Their significance lies in establishing when observed computation represents the underlying dynamical system, with a stronger unconditional statement for the specified Boolean setting.
neurips-1993-observability-of-neural-net.tldr: Observability theorems connect corrupted simulation trajectories to true neural dynamics, with possible small exceptions for analog networks.

paragraphs: This paper studies how neurons should transform their inputs into activation signals in Hopfield-like attractor networks. It extends an analysis of performance over two iterations in networks with Bayesian dynamics that depend on history. The central concern is how the activation rule should use the information available during the network's evolution.

The extension covers input patterns presented to small subsets of neurons, general connectivity architectures, and more efficient use of history. These changes broaden the settings considered by the analysis. They also make the signaling question sensitive to how information enters the network, how neurons connect, and what previous activity contributes to the current response.

The authors find that the optimal activation function has a slanted sigmoid shape. They also provide an intuitive explanation of activation functions with nonmonotone shapes, whose response need not change in only one direction as input changes. The resulting function gives the model some firing properties characteristic of cortical neurons, linking the analytical signaling rule to aspects of biological neuronal behavior.
neurips-1993-optimal-signalling-in-attra.tldr: An extended Bayesian analysis of attractor networks derives a slanted sigmoid activation rule and explains nonmonotone signaling.

paragraphs: This paper studies mathematical questions about feedforward neural networks using the tanh activation function and allowing arbitrarily many layers. Its first question concerns identifiability: whether knowing everything about a network's input-output behavior determines the network that produces it. The objects to be recovered include the architecture, weights, and thresholds.

Subject to technical qualifications, the authors state that complete knowledge of outputs for arbitrary inputs uniquely specifies those objects. The completeness assumption is central to the claim: the theorem concerns the entire input-output mapping. It establishes a relationship between observable function and internal network specification under the paper's mathematical conditions.

The second stated theorem concerns the error surface for a generic training problem. It says that there are only finitely many critical points, meaning points where the error surface is stationary. Together, the results address two forms of mathematical structure: how a network is determined by its behavior and how stationary training configurations are organized. Both claims retain the technical and generic-case qualifications stated in the abstract.
neurips-1993-recovering-a-feed-forward-n.tldr: Qualified theorems establish identifiability from complete outputs and finitely many training-error critical points for generic tanh networks.

paragraphs: This paper tackles ambiguous motion estimates near image edges during optical flow reconstruction. It identifies two sources: the aperture problem and occlusion. In the occlusion case, pixels on both sides of an intensity boundary can receive the same velocity estimate and confidence even though the measurement is correct only on the nonoccluded side.

The proposed method introduces an uncertainty field associated with both motion estimates and their confidence measures. This makes uncertainty part of the reconstruction rather than relying on confidence alone. The authors observe that confidence is high at intensity edges and higher on their convex sides, described as inside corners, than on their concave sides.

Coupled Markov random fields resolve the ambiguities through local interactions. This provides a way for neighboring evidence, uncertainty, and motion estimates to influence one another. The stated outcome is detection of motion in image regions with strong global convexity. The contribution connects local edge ambiguity with a coordinated representation that can support motion detection across larger regions.
neurips-1993-resolving-motion-ambiguitie.tldr: Coupled Markov random fields use explicit uncertainty to resolve edge-related motion ambiguities and detect motion in globally convex regions.

paragraphs: This paper introduces GNARL, an evolutionary program for discovering recurrent neural networks without fixing their structure in advance. The search concerns both how a network is connected and how it behaves. Because recurrent networks have internal dynamics, changing their structure can change the patterns of activity through which they perform a task.

GNARL maintains a population of networks and uses unsupervised feedback from a fitness function to guide the search. This differs from procedures organized around progressively adding or removing network components. Its modifications include Gaussian changes to connection weights and changes to structure, with annealing used in generating both kinds of variation.

The authors apply the program to a complex search-and-collection task. The resulting demonstration shows that it can induce networks with complex internal dynamics. This supports the central premise that evolutionary search over structure and weights can produce recurrent behavior suited to a demanding task. The reported contribution combines an unconstrained structural search method with evidence that the method can discover dynamically rich networks.
neurips-1993-structural-and-behavioral-e.tldr: GNARL evolves recurrent network structures and weights, producing complex internal dynamics for a search-and-collection task.

paragraphs: This paper presents a radial basis function network that grows during supervised learning and supports both classification and regression. Its units have centers and widths that determine their responses to inputs. Center locations are continually adjusted through soft competitive learning, while widths are determined from distances to neighboring units in the network's topology.

The method also tracks where prediction errors occur. It accumulates error locally and uses that information to decide where to insert the next unit. Network growth is therefore directed toward parts of the problem that need additional representational capacity, connecting structural expansion to the supervised learning objective.

For classification, this process places units near class boundaries rather than primarily near peaks in the frequency of observed inputs. That distinction matters because separating classes can require attention to boundaries even when they are not the most densely populated regions. The authors report examples requiring few training epochs and showing apparently strong generalization, presenting these as evidence for the error-guided growth strategy.
neurips-1993-supervised-learning-with-gr.tldr: A growing radial basis function network uses local error to add units near difficult regions such as class boundaries.

paragraphs: This paper trains neural networks to evaluate Go positions using temporal difference learning. The motivation is that Go's many possible moves make tree search difficult, while interactions across space and time complicate position evaluation. Learning an evaluation function offers an alternative to relying on the extensive manually supplied knowledge required by conventional Go programs.

The approach combines architectures that reflect the board's spatial organization with training that exposes networks to competent but unlabeled play. Spatial organization applies to both inputs and reinforcement signals. The authors report that these choices produce much better performance than undifferentiated networks trained only through self-play, making architecture and training experience central to the result.

A network with fewer than 500 weights learned an evaluation function within 3,000 games on a 9-by-9 board. Coupled to a primitive one-ply search, it defeated a commercial Go program at a low playing level. This demonstrates useful learned position evaluation in the stated setting, with the shallow search relying on the network's assessment of positions.
neurips-1993-temporal-difference-learnin.tldr: Spatially organized networks trained with temporal differences and competent play learn useful Go evaluation with fewer than 500 weights.

paragraphs: This paper develops a method for locating two-dimensional objects after rigid transformations, which change placement or orientation while preserving shape. The approach uses mean field theory and produces a coarse-to-fine correlation-matching algorithm. Its purpose is to find an alignment between object descriptions by refining the matching process across levels of detail.

The authors begin with synthetic point data and derive an objective function for matching points. They then extend the construction to line segments by treating each segment as a dense collection of points. Approximating that collection with a sum of Gaussians makes the resulting line-segment matching objective tractable.

The algorithm is tested on real images by extracting line segments and matching them. This links the mathematical point-matching formulation to an image representation used in the reported tests. The contribution is the chain from a mean-field formulation to a manageable segment objective and then to object localization in images, within the stated setting of rigidly transformed two-dimensional objects.
neurips-1993-two-dimensional-object-loca.tldr: A mean-field matching method locates rigidly transformed two-dimensional objects through coarse-to-fine alignment of points and line segments.

paragraphs: This paper addresses the computational difficulty of dynamic programming for nonlinear planning and control. A value function represents the future consequences of actions, making it useful for choosing what to do now. Computing such functions generally is intractable, so the authors seek to use fast local optimization within a broader global procedure.

Their method uses second-order trajectory optimization to produce locally optimal plans together with local models of the value function and its derivatives. These pieces describe how future cost behaves around particular plans. The crucial additional step is maintaining global consistency among the local value-function models, allowing separate local computations to contribute to a coherent overall solution.

The authors state that this consistency guarantees global optimality of the resulting plans up to the resolution of their search procedures. That resolution qualification defines the precision of the guarantee. The approach shows how optimizers that provide local answers can accelerate construction or learning of a globally optimal value function, enabling more complex planning and control problems to be addressed.
neurips-1993-using-local-trajectory-opti.tldr: Globally consistent local value models let fast trajectory optimizers support dynamic programming with optimality limited by search resolution.

paragraphs: This paper describes Wattle, a low-power analog neural network chip intended to classify intracardiac electrograms within an implantable pacemaker or defibrillator system. It implements a three-layer perceptron with 10 input, 6 hidden, and 4 output units. The hardware uses multiplying digital-to-analog converter synapses and switched-capacitor neurons fabricated in a 1.2 μm CMOS process.

The on-chip neurons provide individually variable gain, allowing each neuron's response to be adjusted. The design also reduces energy per connection relative to previous designs. These features connect the chip's learning capabilities with the low-power requirements of its intended application, where neural classification is one component of an integrated device.

Measurements indicate that an energy cost of 10 pJ per connection is achievable within an integrated system. Wattle was successfully trained with the chip in the learning loop on four-input parity and electrogram morphology classification tasks. These results establish trainability on both a parity problem and the signal-shape classification problem relevant to the proposed application.
neurips-1993-wattle-a-trainable-gain-ana.tldr: Wattle is a trainable low-power analog neural chip designed for cardiac signal classification, with measurements indicating 10 pJ per connection.
